question.problem:
The entry ${a}_{21}^{′}$ in the inverse of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & k & 2 \\ 1 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}]$
equals $2.$ Find the value of $k.$

current_example.problem:
The entry $a'_{31}$ in the inverse of the matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14130016/assets/d7b66fc70a215af76358337569fa03473399c954f3232d4b8884ad757b330a9c.svg) 
equals $1$. Find the value of $k$.
current_example.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the determinant of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=|\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & -2 \\ -2 & k & 0 \\ -1 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}| & =3|\begin{aligned}k & 0 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}|-2|\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}|+(-2)|\begin{aligned}-2 & k \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =3(3k-0)-2(-6-0)-2(6+k) \\  & =9k+12-12-2k \\  & =7k.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want the entry $a'_{31}$ in $A^{-1},$ we need to know the value of $c_{13}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{13} & =(-1)^{1+3}|\begin{aligned}-2 & k \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2 & k \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =6+k.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since $A^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{\det (A)}C^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{31}^{′} & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{13} \\  & =\frac{1}{7k}\cdot (6+k) \\  & =\frac{6+k}{7k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are told that $a'_{31}=1$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{6+k}{7k} & =1 \\ 6+k & =7k \\ 6 & =6k \\ k & =1.\end{aligned}
$$
